title: Watertown panko plant agrees to stop pumping so much alcohol into the air
summary: A Chicago company that makes panko breadcrumbs at a plant on Grove Street in Watertown has agreed to pay a nearly $3 million "civil penalty" and to install equipment to capture more of the alcohol that breadcrumb production naturally produces rather than letting it escape into the air. State regulators say as much as nine times more ethanol was billowing into the air from panko production than allowed under a 2014 agreement with environmental regulators. The ethanol, a "volatile organic compound" produced by the yeast that help turn dough into bread suitable for bread crumbs is not by itself harmful to people, but when released as a gas during production, in particular, during baking, it can then break down in the presence of sunlight into ozone, a key component of ground-level smog. In a lawsuit filed in Suffolk Superior Court on Wednesday, the state charges that Newly Weds Foods kept on blowing excessive amounts of the gas into the air from its 169,000-square-foot plant even after it realized it was only reporting the ethanol produced by yeast-enlarged dough balls were baked, but not the ethanol the yeast released while busy expanding smaller dough balls into larger ones, or when the baked dough balls were crushed and then heated to dry them out into flaky crumbs ready for packaging. Without acknowledging it was actually doing anything wrong, the company - which takes credit for introducing panko bread crumbs to the US market in 1977 - agreed to a settlement in which it would install equipment to capture a significant amount of the panko-produced ethanol - and would pay more than $2.9 million as a "civil penalty." Some $1.3 million of that would go into the state's environmental justice fund , which is aimed at environmental improvements in areas with large numbers of "disadvantaged" residents. The settlement has to be approved by a judge before it goes into effect. According to the state, Newly Weds agreed to a state plan in 2014 to limit its monthly ethanol emissions to a maximum of 2.3 tons a month - and a total of 17.9 tons over a 12-month period - based on Newly Wed's estimate that creating flaky panko breadcrumbs would generate about 6.54 pounds of ethanol an hour. But, the state says: Since at least June 1, 2023, after emissions testing at the Facility, Newly Weds has known that the Facility's total JBC [Japanese bread crumbs] process VOC emissions significantly exceed the estimates it provided as part of its 2014 Plan Approval application and that the Facility is emitting VOCs in excess of its permitted limits. On June 1, 2023, Newly Weds knew that the combined outlet ethanol emission rate for the Facility's JBC Ovens and JBC Dryer was 17.6 pounds per hour, including 13.7 pounds per hour for the JBC Ovens and 3.9 pounds per hour for the JBC Dryer, rather than the approximately 6.54 pounds per hour that Newly Weds submitted in its 2014 Plan Application, which was for the JBC oven alone. As a result, all VOC emissions that Newly Weds has reported to DEP using these emissions measurements and emission factors have been inaccurate. The state adds that in on June 7, 2023, Newly Weds met with state regulators and agreed to install a " regenerative thermal oxidizer " - in which ethanol would be captured and heated to upwards of 1,500 degrees, breaking it down to carbon dioxide and water vapor - then didn't. Under the terms of the proposed consent order, Newly Weds would have until Sept. 30, 2027 to install the device.
